title: Blindspots 2 Bodhicitta
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona returns to the story of Naropa and Vajrayogini, in which Naropa assures her that he knows the inner meaning of the teachings and is deluded, as a way into blind spots. Heigaku tells of a heart-attack patient who revives amid a full code team and asks his nurse, "Where the hell is my glass of water?" Bodhicitta, the simple wish for all beings to be happy, becomes the tool, like a pinprick of light through black paper, with Pema Chödrön's fresh looking and Thanissara's practice of the vow as next steps. Everyone then opens an envelope holding an object from nature and writes a conversation with it on an index card about the happiness of all beings.

sentences.text: So we studied the story of Naropa's encounter with Vajrayogini, enlightened energy in female form, and her asking him about the teachings.
He says he's familiar with the teachings and she's happy about that, and then she says, "Well, do you know the inner meaning?" and he assures her, deluded, that he does.
It's a good example of blind spots.
Over this last week we've been looking for how we might see our own blind spots, and from the discussion, I think we don't have a shortage of them.
The next question is, how do we go from there?
Is just following a teacher going to lead us out of our blind spots?
Well, maybe not.
This week I took a CPR refresher course.
It's part of my work.
We took the basic life support.
One of the fellow students told a story about a code that she had responded to the previous week.
A patient asked his nurse for a glass of water, and just as the nurse was leaving the room, the patient had a heart attack.
She heard the heart monitor go into alarm and she ran back into the room and started doing chest compressions.
She called for help, and somebody came and did ventilation.
Pretty soon after that the code response team showed up and put the patient on advanced life support, hooked up a defibrillator and got the patient's heart started again, and got oxygen hooked up.
As the oxygenated blood started returning to the patient's brain, the patient regained consciousness and looked around the room.
He saw all of these medical professionals in the room with him, recognized the familiar face of his nurse, turned to her and said, "Where the hell is my glass of water?"
So there's a blind spot there.
And I think that's me.
Yeah, that could be me.
How often is somebody going through some traumatic ordeal, probably for my benefit?
And there I am again: "Where the hell is my glass of water?"
Another thing we studied in the basic life support class is response to choking.
When we're choking we're not getting oxygen and our brains don't function as well as they do otherwise, so we sometimes return to our basic instincts.
In the last class we talked about some gender differences, neuropsychological differences between men and women.
What was interesting from the class is a difference when people are not thinking clearly and they're choking in a restaurant.
We don't always do the universal choking sign.
There's a tendency for people to get up and leave the table, but where women go and where men go is different.
When women are choking and get up from the table, they tend to go to the ladies' room.
When men are choking and get up from the table in a restaurant, they tend to head outside.
So that's just an interesting difference.
When the paramedics come, they often find the man passed out by his car, as if there's something in his car that he's going to be able to do.
That's an idea: when one gets up and goes to the restroom real quickly without saying anything, and their friend thinks about following them, maybe it's a good idea.
So another tool that we can rely on as we attempt to navigate or deal with our blind spots is bodhicitta.
The literal translation of bodhicitta is awakened heart or awakening impulse.
Would you like all beings to be happy?
Apart from any benefit or detriment to yourself, do you have the desire for all beings to be happy?
Of course we do.
And that fundamentally is bodhicitta.
That simple, selfless desire for joy in the world is the foundation from which all practice springs forth.
By the very act, the sutras tell us, of that desire arising within you for the benefit of others, a causal chain is set in motion that leads to the liberation of all beings from suffering.
When such a desire arises for a glimpse of a moment in one human being, then 10,000 Buddhas in every atom raise a tremendous cry of celebration.
The hurrah rings out across 10,000 universes in the ten directions.
When I asked you just now if you wanted other beings to be happy, did you feel that cry go out across the universe?
That's true.
Dedicating our lives to renunciation of our habits and eliminating the suffering of others feels daunting.
We might admire this quality in a few select heroes but never endeavor so much work ourselves.
But that's not what's present.
That's not what this calling of bodhicitta is.
We're just talking about a twinge of generosity.
We know we can do that.
We may not know we can maintain a continuous mental state of infinite generosity to all beings, but unless you're fully enlightened, don't worry about that.
You do know with great confidence that on occasion you desire happiness for all.
That is no insignificant matter.
It is the root of all future practice.
Pema Chodron jokes that bodhicitta is what we have been studying all along, since the first moment you took a second look at Buddhism.
Galen Godwin defines bodhicitta as the mind that wants to awaken to cause and effect, the mind that wants to awaken for the benefit of all beings.
We already have this loving heart from birth.
That is our nature.
From before our birth, from before the birth of our parents.
But the loving heart gets obscured.
We paper over it with our confusions and our fears.
The five hindrances we have studied all impede our perception of the brilliant compassion residing at the core of our being: desire and aversion, restlessness and fogginess and doubt.
Noticing and feeling our desire for all beings to be happy is like poking a needle hole in the black paper covering our generous Buddha nature, and through that pinprick hole the light pours out.
The ancient teachings of the seven factors of awakening and the five hindrances are critical to working with what we find in our mind.
They are critical to deepening our walk with the way as we continuously return to the breath in our sitting practice.
Our potential to be a part of the benefit to the world has no basis without that practice.
Yet the Mahayana teachings call for us to go beyond that too: to practice for the sake of others, not to bow out of this challenging life while there are still beings suffering.
The first step on that Bodhisattva path, the first step in the liberation of all beings, is the simple blossom of bodhicitta, available to us at any moment.
So we have this desire.
Then what?
Pema Chodron focuses on the aspect of not knowing.
Nourished by bodhicitta, from the desire we can open to the possibility that the world is not as we know it to be.
When experience arises, we can move from predefined, assumed, associated thoughts, "Oh yes, I know this broken record," to look more closely, with the willingness to see what we didn't see before.
When meditation doesn't feel fresh, we can invite the possibility of seeing from a different perspective the thought that seems to match our memory.
We can invite in a beginner's mind, not as a struggle or even an effort, but just a commitment to really look more closely at just what it is that is arising.
And if we misstep and fall into patterned thinking: okay, here's another opportunity, right now, to look closely with the thought, maybe this isn't exactly what I expected it to be.
Jenny Wilkes stresses that loving kindness is not an emotion but an attitude.
It's not that we can dive right in and say, "I love this anguish I have regarding my family," or "I'm so happy to have this pain in my knees."
Who can do that?
And if they can, what truth are they missing out on?
But we can muster an attitude of welcome, of gentleness, to what arises.
Aversion is still there, but so is empathy with the object of the aversion.
Maybe someone is causing us great difficulty.
We don't ignore the difficulty, but we recognize that they also suffer and want to be happy.
She also observes that bodhicitta is developed through our many practices, all of the practices you have heard about and worked with since your first moment of practice.
Once you accept that a basic desire for happiness of all beings is something that arises in you, then where do you go from bodhicitta?
Any other dharma talk could just as well be titled the care and feeding of bodhicitta.
We talk about not feeding our demons.
We invite them to sit down with us as welcome old friends.
But we don't feed greed, hate and delusion by choosing lines of thought and action to make them stronger.
Instead we can feed our bodhicitta, feed our desire for awakening for the benefit of all beings, by undertaking practices that strengthen loving kindness in our lives.
When we're ready to go a step further, Thanissara offers us the practice of the vow.
The vow is a formal commitment to continue on this path.
A vow is undertaken with the knowledge that we stray and get lost, but also with the understanding that we are not alone.
We are here supporting each other.
And slowly we will come to directly experience how we are not separate from all beings in our journey to joy and freedom without limit.
So right now, in one moment, what we have is bodhicitta: a simple desire for welfare for others and for ourselves.
This desire can inspire an attitude of fresh looking that might penetrate our blind spots.
Please go now to the table.
Pick up an index card and a pen and select one of the envelopes.
Don't open it up yet.
Just hold it gently and return to your seat.
Now settle into a posture of meditation.
Do you want to live in ease and joy?
Do you want peace?
Do you want to be happy?
Do you want others to live in ease and joy?
Do you want others to live in peace?
Do you want all other beings to be happy?
Hold gently that desire for all beings to be happy.
When other thoughts arise, acknowledge them and return again to the basic desire of bodhicitta.
In the envelope you will find an object from nature.
Go ahead and open the envelopes.
Study the object.
What does it look like?
What components make it up visually?
What colors?
Sharp shapes or round?
What is its temperature?
What is its texture?
What does it bring to mind for you personally?
What deeper connection does it make with your true nature?
You can silently introduce yourself to the object.
After a few minutes of becoming familiar, sit in silence together, continuing the meditation on bodhicitta.
On the card, write down a conversation with the nature object about the happiness of all beings.
Don't try to write complete sentences, and you will not be asked to share these cards.
What questions do you have for the object?
What advice or warnings?
What does it speak back to you?
What is the feeling of the conversation?
And what is the attitude?
What secrets do you learn?
Thank this piece of Buddha for our time spent together, and recognize that the time together continues endlessly.
Maybe there will be some more literal time that you want to spend with the object, or with the million other objects that arise every moment.
